questions.q: What does a one-way ANOVA test, despite its name?
options: Whether the variances of the groups are equal
Whether all group means are equal, by comparing variation between group means with variation within groups
Whether the data are normally distributed
Which pair of groups differs most
questions.why: H₀ is that all group means are equal. It is called analysis of variance because it decides this by comparing two variances. It does not say which pair differs; that needs a post-hoc test.

questions.q: The F-statistic in a one-way ANOVA is…
options: Within-group variance ÷ between-group variance
The sum of all pairwise t-statistics
The largest group mean ÷ the smallest group mean
Between-group variance (MSB) ÷ within-group variance (MSW)
questions.why: F = MSB / MSW: the spread of group means relative to the noise inside groups. Under H₀ both estimate the same noise and F is about 1; real differences push F up. Flipping the ratio would make large differences give small values.

questions.q: Comparing 5 groups by running all 10 pairwise t-tests at α = 0.05, what is the chance of **at least one** false positive if all groups are truly identical (treating the tests as independent)?
options: About 40%
questions.why: 1 − 0.95¹⁰ = 0.40. Each test carries its own 5% risk, and they accumulate. This is why ANOVA (or a correction for multiple comparisons) is used. 5% would hold for a single test only.

questions.q: Four groups of 5 observations give SSB = 60 and SSW = 80. What is the F-statistic?
questions.why: df between = 4 − 1 = 3; df within = 20 − 4 = 16. MSB = 60 / 3 = 20; MSW = 80 / 16 = 5; F = 20 / 5 = 4.0 (p ≈ 0.027). 0.75 divides the sums of squares without their degrees of freedom.

questions.q: After a significant ANOVA on three scripts, Tukey HSD gives: C − A significant, C − B significant, B − A not significant (adjusted p = 0.24). What should the team conclude?
options: Scripts A and B are proven to perform equally
Roll out script C; A and B cannot be told apart with this much data
All three scripts differ
Run more t-tests on A versus B until one is significant
questions.why: C beats both others. Not significant for B − A means the data cannot distinguish them, not that they are equal. Testing repeatedly until something is significant inflates the false-positive rate that Tukey was protecting.

questions.q: A one-way ANOVA on three steel suppliers gives F = 0.145, p = 0.87. What does an F below 1 mean?
options: The group means are even closer together than random noise would typically make them: no evidence of a difference
The calculation must be wrong, since F cannot be below 1
The suppliers differ strongly, in the opposite direction
Supplier quality is perfectly identical
questions.why: F below 1 happens by chance when between-group spread is smaller than within-group noise would typically produce. It gives no evidence of differences, so procurement can choose on other grounds. It does not prove the suppliers are identical, and F, a ratio of variances, has no direction.

questions.q: Using the same data (SSB = 60, SSW = 80), what share of the total variation is explained by group membership (η²)?
questions.why: η² = SSB / SST = 60 / (60 + 80) = 0.43, so group explains 43% of the variation. 0.75 is SSB / SSW, which is not a share of the total; 0.57 is the unexplained share; 4.0 is the F-statistic.

questions.q: In an interview: "How does one-way ANOVA relate to the t-test?"
options: They are unrelated
ANOVA always gives a smaller p-value than a t-test
ANOVA is just a series of t-tests averaged together
With exactly two groups, one-way ANOVA and the equal-variance t-test give the same p-value, with F = t²; ANOVA generalises the t-test to three or more groups
questions.why: For two groups, F equals the square of Student's t and the p-values match. ANOVA does not average pairwise tests; it tests all means at once with a single F, which is how it avoids piling up false positives.
